title: On the steady-state solution of the M/C2(a, b)/s queueing system
contribution: Solves the multiserver bulk-service queue M/C2(a, b)/s exactly by the generalized method of stages: saturated probabilities from s + 1 separated root equations, the rest from a recursion and an (s + 1)-equation linear system, giving closed-form queue-length, FCFS waiting-time, idle-server and batch-size distributions and an O(as^3) algorithm timed step by step.
problem_entry: {SD; AP (shuttle transport) as motivation} Multiserver bulk queues had been solved only with exponential service, read as the field's reluctance to add analytical complexity (p. 2); relaxed to Coxian-2 service under the (a, b) quorum-capacity rule (abstract, p. 2), with a vehicle-dispatching reading and admitted assumption violations in applications (p. 3).
key_idea: Separated form B_i w^n for saturated states; a generating function over the stage-2 occupancy turns the determinantal root condition, which 'leads to rather extreme computational problems', into s + 1 scalar equations with one root in (0, 1) each (Prop. 1, Lemma 2, p. 7); a recursion (Fig. 3) and a linear system of s + 1 equations finish the solution (p. 8); the combination is called 'a new approach' (p. 6).
assumptions: Poisson arrivals, s identical servers, one FCFS line, C2 service, (a, b) rule, rho < 1 (pp. 2, 4-5, 7); C2 justified as covering a wide SCV range yet tractable (p. 4) and by a mechanism: two destination groups give trip SCVs above one (p. 3); Cm possible but 'considerably' costlier (p. 4); no data.
proof_devices: equivalence Eb/C2/s = M/C2(b, b)/s (arrival stages read as customers, customers as groups), which led to Prop. 1; proof only outlined, the Rouche part deferred to the authors' Ek/C2/s paper (pp. 6-7)
generating-function polynomiality forcing an integer exponent, one scalar root equation per index j (Prop. 1, p. 7)
root ordering 0 < w_s < ... < w_0 < 1 (Lemma 2, p. 7), used for root finding and for the geometric tail rate w_0 (Prop. 4, p. 9)

FCFS waiting time split by the state the arriving customer finds, one case via the maximum of independent arrival and departure times; next-event differential equations and Laplace transforms (Prop. 5, pp. 9-11); Little's formula checked (p. 12)
complexity O(as^3) time and O(s^3) memory, Step 3 dominant (p. 13)
experiments: BASIC on a personal computer and FORTRAN on a CYBER 171; per-step times for M/C2(10, 15)/s from 79 ms (s = 1) to 28,232 ms (s = 25), Step 3 dominant (Table III); performance measures by SCV (M/C2(4, 12)/15, rho = 0.9, Lq 50.94 to 202.71) and by quorum a (M/C2(a, 10)/5) (Tables I-II); agreement with Sim-Templeton for M/M(a, b)/s; no failures reported (p. 13).
positioning: Pollaczek-type complex-variable expressions called 'almost purely formal' and computationally costly (p. 5); multiserver bulk literature confined to exponential service (p. 5); results question Asgharzadeh-Newell's insensitivity conclusion (p. 13).
writing: Five numbered contributions in the introduction (p. 2); self-praise ('impressively low order of computational complexity', p. 2; 'simpler and more elegant', p. 14); the closing 'Ariadne's thread' metaphor (p. 14); numerics framed as an illustration of 'stability and accuracy' (p. 13).
limits_future: C2 only (p. 4); model assumptions may fail in applications (p. 3); cost optimization of dispatching and simple approximations deferred to 'a forthcoming paper' (p. 13); future: Cox's complex transition rates toward a general calculus of rational distributions for multiserver queues (p. 14).

method_links.note: The kept class is an analysable distribution class (C2), not LP or MIO; the separated root equations replace the determinant and keep the algorithm polynomial and in real arithmetic; the boundary (Cm costlier) and measured per-step times are printed. A co-authored SD paper with stated motives.

The field's avoidance of non-exponential multiserver bulk queues is named and the problem reopened, with run times in support; but the reason is a new analytic device, not a tool change, and the old belief is not conceded.
The operator's knob (quorum a) is tabulated against queue length, utilization and batch size (Table II), but no cost or price curve is drawn; the dispatching optimization is deferred.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Cox's stage representation, which covers every pdf with rational Laplace transform and approximates any pdf, keeps the analysis finite; C2 covers a wide SCV range yet stays tractable; recurs from S239 and S346 (card s01).

transferable: Replace a high-degree determinantal root condition by a generating function over the phase index; requiring it to be a polynomial forces an integer exponent and splits the condition into one scalar equation per root (p. 7).
Identify a new bulk model with a solved one by reading Erlang arrival stages as customers and customers as groups, then reuse the solved model's root theorem (pp. 6-7).
Use a proven ordering of the roots twice: to speed up root finding and to read the geometric tail rate off the largest root (pp. 7, 9).
Report execution time per algorithm step across problem sizes so that the bottleneck is visible (Table III, p. 13).

We believe that the combination of separation of variables and the use of generating functions is a new approach, which seems to give very promising results.

title: The Probabilistic Minimum Spanning Tree, Part II: Probabilistic Analysis and Asymptotic Results
contribution: Compares the a priori PMST strategy with MST and Steiner re-optimization probabilistically: in the random Euclidean model the optimal PMST's expected length is claimed asymptotically equal to MST re-optimization and within a constant (15% under the Gilbert-Pollak conjecture) of Steiner re-optimization; in the random length model it lies between p*zeta(3) and zeta(3), with p*zeta(3) conjectured.
problem_entry: {SD; IO} After Part I proved the PMST NP-complete, ask whether the robust (network unchanged), real-time (O(n) update) a priori tree loses much against re-solving each instance for the MST or the Steiner tree (pp. 8-9); answered in the random Euclidean and random length models with one common presence probability p (p. 9).
key_idea: Compare expectations, not instances (p. 27): concentrate the number of present points by a Chernoff bound so deterministic limit theorems apply (Thm 1, pp. 13-15); show the optimal PMST is a subadditive Euclidean functional, apply Steele's theory and identify its constant (Thm 2, pp. 15-22); carry Frieze's zeta(3) limit to re-optimization and bound the PMST (pp. 23-25).
assumptions: Independent presence with one common p, assumed because the analysis is asymptotic in n (p. 9); uniform points in the unit square or uniform arc costs (p. 9); cases np -> infinity and np -> 0 (pp. 15, 23); no data.
proof_devices: Chernoff concentration of the number of present points around np, deterministic limits on the bulk (pp. 13-14, 20-21, 24-25)

subadditivity by construction: optimal PMST per subsquare, one always-present ('black') leaf representative each, MST on the representatives (p. 17); an induction bounds the extra expected length by the longest edge times (1 - p)/p (pp. 18-19); monotonicity asserted as clear (p. 16)
constant identified by a scaling law beta(p) = A*sqrt(p) plus bounds valid for every p, closed by letting p -> 1 (pp. 20-22)
15% to Steiner only 'If we adopt the Gilbert and Pollak [8] conjecture' (p. 22)
random length model: p*zeta(3) <= E[L_Tp] <= zeta(3) (Prop. 4, p. 25); Conjecture 5 (p. 26)
positioning: Places itself in three literatures: random Euclidean probabilistic analysis (Beardwood-Halton-Hammersley, Karp, Steele), random length models (Karp, Frieze, Steele) and probabilistic combinatorial optimization (Jaillet's PTSP thesis and his own thesis) (pp. 10-12).
writing: Question-led introduction (p. 9); 'Surprisingly' for the main equality (p. 9); the abstract and introduction state a strict ordering in the random length model (pp. 6, 10) that the conclusion hedges as 'at least as good (we conjecture strictly better)' (p. 27): Tension T6.
limits_future: Steiner re-optimization not analysed in the random length model for lack of sharp theorems; the PMST is suboptimal on individual instances; Conjecture 5 open (p. 26). The 1990 journal version (S148) finds the functional not monotone, proves only approximate monotonicity, asserts only a constant c(p, d), sums up 'within constant factors' and weakens random-length convergence to 'in probability' (S148 pp. 1, 24-25, 28-30).

method_links.note: The price of a robust, real-time a priori strategy is computed against re-solving: asymptotically zero against MST re-optimization and about 15% against Steiner under a conjecture; no knob, p is data (as in S148, card s01).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The O(n)-updatable a priori tree is compared with MST and Steiner re-optimization by asymptotic expectations; recurs from S038 and S017 (card c01) and S148 (card s01).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: carry deterministic devices into the stochastic version and measure what survives
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Steele's subadditive Euclidean functional theory is carried over; subadditivity must be re-proved ('It is not clear that the subadditivity property holds'), and the monotonicity asserted here fails per the journal version (S148 p. 25).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: claim narrowed from working paper to journal
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The working paper's exact constant (PMST asymptotically equal to MST re-optimization) and almost-sure random-length limits become 'within constant factors' and convergence 'in probability' in the 1990 journal version, which also states that the functional is not monotone (S148 pp. 1, 24-25, 28-30).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: limit case of the new parameter pins an unknown constant
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The PMST constant is written as A*sqrt(p) with A independent of p; bounds valid for every p meet as p -> 1, giving the MST constant; close to s01's 'limit cases of the new parameter locate the hardness' (S148).

transferable: For expectations over random sub-instances, condition on the number of present points, discard counts outside np(1 +/- eps) with a Chernoff bound, and apply the deterministic limit theorem to the rest (pp. 13-14, 24-25).
Prove subadditivity of an a priori structure by gluing optimal pieces through always-present representatives and bounding the extra expected length the representatives cause (pp. 16-20).
Identify an unknown limit constant by its scaling law plus bounds that hold for every parameter value, then send the parameter to the value where the bounds meet (pp. 20-22).
Name the conjecture inside any sentence whose number rests on it (p. 22).

quotes.text: How does the idea of having an a priori solution to a combinatorial optimization problem compare with re-optimization strategies in terms of performance?

It is quite surprising to find that the PMST strategy is asymptotically equivalent in terms of performance to the MST re-optimization strategy in the random Euclidean model and at least as good (we conjecture strictly better) in the random length model.

title: Traveling salesman facility location problems
contribution: Read in the 1988 working-paper version: proves that under the triangle inequality the facility belongs at an always-present node, tightens the incumbent TSFLP heuristic's worst-case bound to (1 - p_i*)/2, reduces the a priori version (PTSFLP) to n PTSPs, gives an O(n^2) spacefilling-curve heuristic within O(log n) of both problems, and shows asymptotically that location does not matter and that the a priori problem matches re-optimization.
problem_entry: {IO + SD; AP (locating a service unit) as motivation} Berman and Simchi-Levi's TSFLP heuristic (worst-case error 1/2) and O(n^3) algorithm for a given a priori tour (WP pp. 4, 7, 16); the turning argument is the planner's: a good location without an estimate of its cost (WP p. 11), since g(i) needs 2^n NP-hard tours (WP p. 21).
key_idea: Exchange argument for an always-present node (Thm 1); a sharper analysis of the incumbent heuristic (Thm 4); the PTSFLP as n PTSPs by setting the candidate's probability to 1; a sorted (spacefilling-curve) a priori tour is consistent with the skipping rule 'because sorting has the property of preserving the order', so the O(log n) TSP guarantee holds on every instance (Thm 5), and its expected cost is known in closed form (WP pp. 6-16).
assumptions: Independent presence p_i (WP p. 6); triangle inequality for Thms 1 and 4, Thm 1 stated to fail without it (WP p. 7); facility at a node, optimal by Berman-Simchi-Levi (WP pp. 6, 12); Euclidean points for the heuristic; equal p and uniform points for the asymptotics (WP p. 17); no data.
proof_devices: pairwise exchange g(i) - g(j) = (1 - p_j) sum p(S)[L(S+i) - L(S+i+j)] <= 0 under the triangle inequality (Thm 1, WP pp. 6-7)

two-sided bound between the true objective and the surrogate L(S) + 2d(i, S) via a Hamiltonian-path argument (Prop. 3, WP pp. 9-10), giving the (1 - p_i*)/2 bound, '25% instead of 50%' at p = 1/2 (Thm 4, WP pp. 10-11)
order preservation of sorting transfers the Platzman-Bartholdi O(log n) ratio to every instance (Thm 5, WP pp. 14-15)
incremental update: consecutive candidates differ in two probability entries, so each expected cost follows from the previous one in O(n): O(n^3) -> O(n^2) (WP p. 16)
asymptotics: Thm 7 by an O(1) additive term against sqrt(n); Thm 8 'using exactly the same type of proof as in [6]'; Thm 9 from the thesis (WP pp. 18-20)
experiments: none in this paper; Thm 9's 25% uses an empirical beta_1 = 0.956 and 'the conjectured value' beta_TSP = 0.765 (WP p. 20); the conclusion cites thesis PTSP heuristics within 2-5% of the predicted cost on random problems (WP pp. 21-22).
positioning: Improves both Berman-Simchi-Levi results (worst-case bound; O(n^3) algorithm) and extends Jaillet's and his own a priori approach to location (WP pp. 4-5, 11, 16).
writing: Results listed in the abstract (WP p. 2); the planner-scenario paragraph as the turn of the argument (WP p. 11); 'an important result' for asymptotic equivalence (WP p. 5); conjectures labelled as such (WP pp. 16-17).
limits_future: Only an O(log n) guarantee; Conjecture 6 (O(1)) rests on Platzman-Bartholdi's conjecture (WP pp. 16-17); the 25% rests on empirical and conjectured constants (WP p. 20); the PTSFLP still needs n PTSPs (WP p. 21). The journal abstract drops the O(1) conjecture, adds a network heuristic and weakens 'asymptotically equivalent' to 'asymptotically very close' (abstracts.json). [inferred] With every p_i = 1 the ratio is the curve heuristic's TSP ratio, so S161's line instances (TR pp. 1, 5) refute Conjecture 6 as stated.

method_links.note: The planner's needs (knowing what the decision costs, getting each day's tour in real time) are the stated reason to replace a heuristic that has a good guarantee by a different problem; but the planner is constructed, with no owner, data or current rule.
The price of the a priori, real-time strategy is measured asymptotically (zero for the optimal PTSFLP, about 25% for the O(n^2) heuristic), not set with a knob.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: PTSFLP (a priori tour, skip absent nodes) against TSFLP (re-optimize daily): asymptotically equivalent, with the a priori version computable in real time and its cost known.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: asymptotic optimality as the warrant for a simple heuristic
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The incumbent heuristic is proved asymptotically optimal (Thm 7), while the location itself is asymptotically irrelevant.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: claim narrowed from working paper to journal
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The WP abstract's O(1) conjecture is absent from the journal abstract, and 'asymptotically equivalent' becomes 'asymptotically very close' (abstracts.json); the conjecture's premise was refuted in S161 (card s01).

transferable: Prove that a facility belongs at a node that always needs a visit by a pairwise exchange of expected tour lengths under the triangle inequality (WP pp. 6-7).
Reduce the joint choice of a location and an a priori tour to n a priori problems by setting each candidate's presence probability to 1 (WP pp. 12-13).
Prefer heuristics whose output is unchanged by the instance's skipping rule (a sort along a curve), so that a worst-case guarantee holds instance by instance (WP pp. 14-15).
When candidates' closed-form expected costs differ in a few probability entries, update incrementally instead of recomputing: O(n^3) -> O(n^2) (WP p. 16).
Ask what the planner can do with a heuristic's output; if it gives no cost estimate, say so and reformulate (WP p. 11).

quotes.text: So the planner would be faced with the rather unusual situation of knowing a good location for the facility, but without knowing the cost of this decision.
because sorting has the property of preserving the order, which is exactly the property of the PTSP strategy as well

title: The dynamic traveling repairman problem
contribution: Working-paper version of the DTRP study: a dynamic, stochastic routing model with waiting time as the objective, light- and heavy-traffic lower bounds over all policies (the heavy-traffic one resting on a conjectured nearest-neighbour bound), the stochastic queue median policy proved optimal in light traffic, and partitioning and TSP-tour policies within constant factors in heavy traffic, with the nearest-neighbour policy simulated.
problem_entry: {SD; AP as motivation} The TSP is 'a deterministic, static approximation' of probabilistic, dynamic problems in which waiting, not travel, is the cost (p. 4); applications (inventory, emergency service, repair, landing sequencing, taxis, sales leads) and five characteristics (pp. 4-5); entry from Psaraftis's dynamic TSP, the traveling repairman problem, a priori optimization ('inherently static') and the stochastic queue median problem (pp. 5-7).
key_idea: Lower bounds for all policies first, then simple policies analysed against them (p. 7): the median-based SQM policy is optimal as lambda -> 0 (Thm 1, p. 17); stable heavy-traffic policies must shrink travel per service, achieved by partitioning into cyclic queues and by TSP tours over batches (pp. 17-26); system time grows like (1 - rho)^-2 because of geometry (p. 14).
assumptions: Square region of area A ('can be relaxed', p. 11); Poisson arrivals, uniform i.i.d. locations, i.i.d. on-site service with known first two moments, unit speed, decisions only at service completions; travel times not i.i.d., so M/G/1 methods do not apply directly (p. 11); the heavy-traffic bound assumes the uniform-points nearest-neighbour bound holds for every stable policy, conjectured but unproved (p. 14); NN needs an assumed constant gamma with 'no analytical guidance' (p. 27); no data.
proof_devices: light-traffic bound: split system time, server at its best a priori position (the median), Little's law (pp. 12-13)
heavy-traffic bound: stability condition, assumed nearest-neighbour bound, Jensen's inequality; 'partly heuristic' (pp. 13-14, 30)
FCFS as M/G/1, Pollaczek-Khinchin valid without mutual independence; light-traffic ratio at most c1/c3 ~ 1.36 (pp. 15-16)
PART1 as an exhaustive symmetric cyclic queue with a projection rule; a stable policy exists for every rho < 1 (Thm 2, p. 19); best m tends to twice its critical value, ratio about 4 (p. 20)
PART2 bracketed between two cyclic queues with customers slid toward or away from the server (pp. 21-22)

TSP policy: batches of N as a GI/G/1 queue with Erlang-N interarrivals, Kingman's bound, BHH tour asymptotics, N reparametrized against its critical value; ratio about 2.1 with beta_TSP ~ 0.72 (pp. 24-26)
experiments: Nearest-neighbour policy simulated by batch means (p. 27; protocol page missing); log-log plot of simulated T_NN against the bound (Fig. 6, p. 28); one numerical example over rho (Figs 7-8): SQM best below rho = 0.05, NN dominant above 0.1, TSP second where its bound is valid (rho > 0.5), PART1 better than PART2 for 0.1 < rho < 0.8 (pp. 28-30).
positioning: Generalizes the stochastic queue median results (Berman, Larson, Odoni; Batta et al.), calling its bound 'somewhat stronger' because it covers all policies (p. 17); places his own a priori optimization among static approaches (p. 6); credits Psaraftis for the problem (p. 31).
writing: Application list ending in a joke about a salesman's leads (p. 5); candid verdicts ('not terribly satisfactory from a practical standpoint', p. 24; 'partly heuristic', p. 30); but the introduction calls the TSP policy's 2.1 'the best provable performance guarantee' although it rests on the conjectured bound (pp. 7, 14): Tension T6.
limits_future: Heavy-traffic bound unproved; NN without a guarantee; one vehicle; 'no single policy dominates for all traffic conditions' (pp. 14, 30); future: multiple vehicles and a rigorous proof of the nearest-neighbour bound (p. 31). The journal version (S016) proves a bound with gamma ~ 0.266, keeps gamma = 1/2 as a conjecture and reports PART's provable factor as about 15, or 4.2 under the conjecture (S016 pp. 7, 9).

method_links.note: The lower bound acts as the certificate and each policy's ratio to it as the gap; the simulated best policy (NN) is not called guaranteed; but the heavy-traffic certificate rests on an unproved assumption while the introduction says 'provable' (Tension T6).
The objective is changed to the real cost (waiting), and policies are designed so that a solvable queue class (M/G/1, cyclic, GI/G/1) applies; the kept class is an analysable queue, not LP or MIO.

title: An analytic approach to a general class of G/G/s queueing systems
contribution: Solves the Coxian queue Ck/Cm/s in closed form by a generalized method of stages: separation of variables and a polynomiality condition on a multivariate generating function give one root equation per server-occupancy vector (the separability property), so saturated system-size probabilities are finite geometric mixtures, with an exact algorithm programmed and tested.
problem_entry: {SD} GI/G/s 'has survived the attacks of many excellent mathematicians and operations researchers' (p. 1); a critical survey finds embedded Markov chains dimension-bound, supplementary variables limited, complex-variable methods costly, and Erlang's stages 'neglected for some time' out of fear of equations 'certainly not more formidable' than the others' (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Markov chain by generalized stages (p. 3); separation of variables for partial difference equations, borrowed from PDE theory (p. 5); an m-variable generating function solved by characteristics, whose polynomiality yields one scalar equation per occupancy vector, each root w satisfying 'a different equation' (pp. 6-8); the root equations involve only the two Laplace transforms (p. 10).
assumptions: Coxian arrivals (k stages) and service (m stages), chosen as versatile and dense in all distributions on (0, infinity) (p. 3); rho < 1; distinct roots assumed: measure-zero failure set, no counterexample found, conjectured always true, proved for m = 2 (p. 10); no data.
proof_devices: separation of variables plus generating-function polynomiality (pp. 5-8)
method of characteristics for a first-order linear PDE; eigenvalues of the stage matrix (Prop. 1, pp. 6-7)
existence of roots by Schauder's fixed point theorem; uniqueness for extreme occupancy vectors by the argument principle (Thm 2, pp. 8-9)
general uniqueness not proved 'using results of the present theory exclusively', closed by combining Thm 2 with Pollaczek's and de Smit's root counts (p. 10)
special cases recovering the G/M/s equation and Ek/C2/s; Rouche for Ek/Em/s (pp. 10-11)
explicit root equations only for m <= 4 (Abel-Ruffini); exponential root count when s and m grow together (p. 12)
experiments: C2/C2/s in FORTRAN on a SUN 3 and Ek/C2/s on a CYBER 171; tested for V^2 up to 100, k up to 50, s up to 40 with internal accuracy checks and agreement with Groenevelt et al. and de Smit; mean-wait tables at rho = 0.9; fast convergence in k to D/C2/s; CPU-time figure by k and s (values not in text); per-step complexity table (pp. 14-16).
positioning: A 'brief critical presentation' of four rival approaches, each with its named limit (pp. 1-2); against purely numerical methods it claims qualitative insight from closed forms (p. 2); credits Pollaczek and de Smit for the uniqueness step (p. 10).
writing: Separates what 'the present theory exclusively' proves from what is borrowed (p. 10); conjectures stated with reasons (pp. 10, 13); first-person stance on testing algorithms (p. 14) and on m = 2 'In the opinion of the author' (p. 12); numerics 'as an illustration of the stability and accuracy' (p. 15).
limits_future: Root uniqueness borrowed, distinctness conjectured (p. 10); exponential growth when s and m grow (pp. 12, 15). Future: exact FCFS waiting times (p. 2), Cox's complex rates, transfer-function order reduction from electrical engineering, and the GI/R/s conjecture (pp. 12-13).

method_links.note: The kept class is the Coxian (rational-transform) class, dense yet finite to analyse, not LP or MIO; the boundary is printed (explicit only for m <= 4, exponential in s and m) and the stop rule's logic appears: measure, then change the device (m = 2, order reduction).

A neglected method is reopened and the field's avoidance contested, backed by programmed and tested algorithms; the old view is called overstated rather than conceded, and no tool-change figure is given. A sole-author SD paper with stated motives, against the Domain Map's 'co-authored papers only' for SD.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Table I gives time and memory per algorithm step (step 3 heaviest); Figure 5 plots CPU seconds against k and s.

Prove existence of roots by a fixed-point theorem on a compact region and uniqueness in extreme cases by the argument principle or Rouche (pp. 8-11).
When your own theory leaves a gap, close it with a known count from a rival method and state which part is borrowed (p. 10).
Test an exact algorithm at extreme parameters (V^2 up to 100, k up to 50, s up to 40) against published tables from rival methods, with internal accuracy checks (p. 15).

In the opinion of the author, in a practical situation the value of m = 2 is a tradeoff between accuracy and simplicity, which has the additional advantage of the rather unexpected real arithmetic.

title: The departure process from a GI/G/1 queue and its applications to the analysis of tandem queues
contribution: Characterizes the GI/G/1 departure process exactly (interdeparture transform, autocorrelations, counting process) by Hilbert factorization, with finite forms when one input has a rational transform, and uses it in an approximate tandem-queue algorithm that assumes a queue's wait independent of its input interval, implemented in Mathematica and checked against published simulations.
problem_entry: {SD; AP (manufacturing, communications) as motivation} Networks need departure processes as inputs; beyond exponential assumptions they are not renewal, exact results are few, and FCFS networks beyond Jackson's have none, so the field turned to approximations (Whitt's QNA, Harrison-Dai) (p. 4).
key_idea: The interdeparture time is the idle time plus the next service time, independent (pp. 5-6); Hilbert factorization of the Lindley process gives its transform; the general Cauchy-integral form is rejected as numerically unstable in favour of R/G/1 and GI/R/1 (Thms 1-2, pp. 7-9); correlations via Cauchy integrals and Keilson's Green's function method (pp. 10-15); tandem queues under Assumption A, which keeps each departure transform rational (pp. 25-27).
assumptions: Single-server FCFS queues; R/R/1 'for tractability purposes' (p. 25); Assumption A (W_i independent of D_i-1): exact for series of M/M/1 queues and renewal departures, otherwise a renewal approximation that keeps the whole interdeparture law (p. 25); no data.
proof_devices: Liouville's theorem on the two analytic half-planes of the factorization; roots located by Rouche (pp. 7-8)
Laurent expansion and Cauchy integrals for the covariance of adjacent interdeparture times (pp. 10-11)
Green's function method (Keilson) for arbitrary lags: homogeneous solution, then compensation (pp. 12-15)
Lagrange implicit-function inversion for M/G/1 and GI/M/1 correlations (pp. 16-20)
symbolic Mathematica checks on M/M/1 (pp. 12, 16, 22)
experiments: Mathematica with Hosono's Laplace inversion; departure correlations near 0.01; two Whitt examples against simulation (E[W1] 1.35 vs 1.360, E[W2] 8.70 vs 8.131; 0.0964 vs 0.096, 0.0265 vs 0.026); answers close to QNA; a four-queue example published without simulation; no run times (pp. 27-29).
positioning: Builds on Burke and Daley; positions against Whitt's renewal and two-moment approximations ('unlike Whitt [12], we use information about the entire interdeparture distribution rather than its first two moments') and the Brownian approach (pp. 4, 25, 28).
writing: The abstract credits 'the direct exploitation of the characteristics of the departure process' (p. 3); 'Surprisingly' for non-vanishing heavy-traffic correlations (p. 18); a 7% gap on E[W2] described as the methods 'differ slightly' (p. 29).
limits_future: 'We were unable to solve the problem exactly' (p. 25), hence Assumption A; inverting the counting-process transforms is 'a nontrivial matter' (p. 22); the number of roots grows along the line (p. 27); no future work stated beyond the published benchmark example (p. 29).

method_links.note: A class-keeping device in queueing form: Assumption A makes each departure transform rational, so the recursion stays in class R; the general closed form is rejected as numerically useless; the growth in the number of roots along the line is printed.
The incumbent (Whitt's two-moment QNA) and published simulations are the opponents, and computed correlations serve as an accuracy indicator; no certificate, and a 7% gap is called slight.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: a posteriori computational justification of a simplifying assumption
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Computed departure autocorrelations near 0.01 are read as almost-renewal departures, so Assumption A is accurate; the example with higher correlations shows the larger gap.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: dense rational-transform class as the tractability device
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: R/G/1 and GI/R/1 give 'computationally very tractable' finite forms where the general solution is numerically unstable; the tandem algorithm stays within rational transforms.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: re-derive classical theorems with the new device
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Zero covariance of M/M/1 departures (Burke) and the M/M/1 counting-process formulas are checked symbolically.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: report where the algorithm spends its time, by step
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Step 1 (root finding) is named the bottleneck and the number of roots counted for a line of Q queues.

transferable: Write the interdeparture time as the idle time plus the next service time, which are independent, so that its transform follows from the waiting-time factorization (pp. 5-6).
When a general closed form is numerically unstable, restrict one input distribution to rational transforms to obtain finite root sums (p. 7).
In a decomposition approximation, compute the dependence you neglect (here departure autocorrelations) and report it beside each result as an accuracy indicator (pp. 27-29).
Publish a fully specified example without simulation so that others can benchmark against it (p. 29).

quotes.text: Although this a result in closed form, we do not believe that it is numerically useful, since the inversion of such a transform is numerically unstable due to the multiple branch points in the integrand.

As it is quite difficult to find reliable simulation results in the literature we present a random example so that researchers can compare these results with simulation results and with their methods.

title: Relations between the prearrival and postdeparture state probabilities and the FCFS waiting time distribution in the Ek/G/s queue
contribution: Generalizes Burke's theorem to processes with jumps of size k, links the postdeparture stage probabilities of the Ek/G/s queue to its FCFS waiting-time density by a probabilistic argument, and, with the Ck/Cm/s closed forms, obtains the Ek/Cm/s waiting-time density as a finite sum of exponentials, computed for Ek/C2/s up to 100 servers.
problem_entry: {SD} Exact multiserver waiting-time distributions 'present substantial difficulties' (p. 1), and non-exponential service makes them 'really challenging' (p. 2); the gap is the step from known stationary stage probabilities to the FCFS waiting time (p. 1).
key_idea: Burke's pre-jump/post-jump equality generalized via Cesaro limits (Thms 1-2, pp. 3-6); a test-customer argument: the arrival stages accumulated behind the customer now entering service arrived during that customer's wait, and stage arrivals are Poisson, so the postdeparture stage pmf determines the waiting-time density (Thm 3, p. 8); stationary -> postdeparture -> waiting time (p. 9).
assumptions: Erlang-k arrivals by Kendall's stage decomposition, general then Coxian service, s servers, FCFS, rho < 1; Whitt's finite-busy-period conditions hold automatically (pp. 6-7); the method needs the stage-count distribution (p. 1); no data.
proof_devices: Cesaro averages for the periodic case k >= 2, where ordinary limits do not exist (p. 3)
generating-function relation k(1 - z)G-(z) = (1 - z^k)G+(z) (Thm 1, p. 4); Thm 2 sketched by similarity (pp. 5-6)
test-customer argument with Poisson stage arrivals at rate k*lambda (Thm 3, p. 8), extending Haji-Newell's M/G/s relation
'Poisson arrivals see time averages' for the stage process (Thm 4, pp. 8-9); closed form via S168's Ck/Cm/s results (pp. 10-11); real distinct roots in (0, 1) for Ek/C2/s (p. 12)
experiments: FORTRAN on a SUN 3 after 'meticulous tests'; O(s^2) memory, O(ks^3) time; s up to 100 and k up to 20 in seconds, memory limits beyond in a time-sharing environment; rho up to 0.99 and C^2 up to 100; Figures 2-5 plot Pr{Tq > t} against s, C^2, k and rho; no comparison with other methods (pp. 12-14).
positioning: Corrects the history of Burke's theorem as an associate editor pointed out and credits Hebuterne's independent results, pointed out by referees (pp. 3, 14); extends Haji-Newell (p. 8); lists exact multiserver results by Pollaczek, de Smit, Ishikawa and Ramaswami-Lucantoni (p. 2).
writing: Compact abstract; 'an exact probabilistic method' as the selling point (p. 1); numerics 'Merely as an illustration of the stability and accuracy' (p. 14), the same frame as S168 (p. 15) and S291 (p. 13).
limits_future: Erlang arrivals only; requires the stage distribution (p. 1); memory boundary at higher s and k (p. 14); no conclusion or future-work section.

method_links.note: The Coxian class keeps the waiting time a finite exponential mixture (a class kept, not LP or MIO); the boundary is reported as measured (seconds at s = 100, k = 20; memory beyond), an early instance of Heuristic 4's printed memory limits.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: subsume the incumbent as a special case
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Burke's theorem and Haji and Newell's M/G/s relation become special cases of the jump-size-k theorems and the Ek/G/s relation.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: dense rational-transform class as the tractability device
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The Coxian representation of the rational class, dense in all distributions on (0, infinity), yields a finite sum of exponentials for the waiting time.

transferable: When a jump process is periodic (jumps of size k), relate pre-jump and post-jump distributions through Cesaro limits instead of ordinary limits (pp. 3-4).
Link a post-departure count to a waiting-time law by a test-customer argument: what accumulated behind the customer now entering service arrived during that customer's wait (p. 8).
Report the scale reached and the resource that ran out (here memory) in the body of the paper (p. 14).

quotes.text: In our experiments we went up to s = 100 and k = 20 and the answer was found in a few seconds.
Since the experiments were run in a time-sharing environment, memory started to become a problem for higher values.

title: On the characteristic equation of general queueing systems
contribution: Extends the method of stages to arbitrary distributions with supplementary variables and operators, showing that queues with heterogeneous servers, several arrival streams, bulk moves and feedback are governed by one characteristic equation whose roots make queue lengths geometric and waiting times exponential mixtures, finite when service is in the rational class.
problem_entry: {SD} 'numerous papers' analyse specific queues through roots of a nonlinear equation (abstract, p. 3); exact analyses assume homogeneous servers and one renewal stream (p. 4); aim: the solution structure for multistream, heterogeneous, bulk and feedback queues, and a unification of the field (pp. 3-4).
key_idea: Kolmogorov equations with elapsed-time supplementary variables and hazard rates, written with operators; separation of variables; the characteristic equation read off the eigenfunctions of each arrival or service operator (Lemma 1, pp. 4-7); physically, one operator per independent process, and the characteristic equation says the spectrum of their sum is zero (pp. 12-14).
assumptions: Systems starting empty for the transient analysis, FCFS for waiting times (pp. 5, 9); renewal arrival streams, heterogeneous servers (p. 9); separated product form assumed as the general solution (p. 6); finitely many terms only for rational service transforms (pp. 8, 11); no data.
proof_devices: operator form of the Kolmogorov equations with supplementary variables; Laplace transform in t (pp. 5-6)
eigenfunctions of the arrival and service operators and their characteristic equation (Lemma 1, pp. 6-7)
Rouche for the GI/R/1 root count (exactly k roots); a continuum of roots indexed by u for GI/G/1, asserted without a completeness argument (my reading) (Thm 1, p. 8)
distributional Little's law for waiting-time densities and tails (pp. 9, 11)
Keilson's compensation method and the operator rule for bulk and feedback queues (pp. 13-15)
experiments: none (one remark from experience: root finding is 'computationally quite easy' and the linear system takes most of the time, p. 12)
positioning: Unifies results of Ramaswami-Lucantoni, de Smit, his own R/R/m and Yu (p. 4); agrees with his R/R/m and generalizes Takahashi's Ph/Ph/c asymptotics (p. 11); agrees with Chaudhry, Harris and Marchal on root finding (p. 12).
writing: Claims hedged as 'structural' and 'potentially' algorithmic (pp. 3, 4, 16); 'This queue is notorious for its difficulty' (p. 9); the operator method sold as 'one of the most commonly used tools in modern physics' (pp. 12-13).
limits_future: Structural only for arbitrary distributions; no implemented algorithm; the linear system 'becomes very large very quickly' (p. 12); future: a finite algorithm for the rational class (p. 16).

method_links.note: One formulation (the characteristic equation) covers a family that classical methods treat case by case; the boundary is printed (finite only in class R; the linear system is the bottleneck), but nothing is implemented or measured here.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: unify-then-extend
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: GI/G/1 and the multistream heterogeneous queue are brought under one characteristic equation, then extended to bulk arrivals, bulk service and feedback by the operator rule.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: subsume the incumbent as a special case
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Theorem 2 agrees with his R/R/m results and generalizes Takahashi's Ph/Ph/c tail asymptotics.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: import a solution device from physics or engineering
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The generator-spectrum method, 'one of the most commonly used tools in modern physics', is used to write characteristic equations directly; S168 proposes transfer-function order reduction from electrical engineering (S168 p. 12).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: report where the algorithm spends its time, by step
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: For the rational class the time goes to the linear system, not the roots, per experience with R/R/m.

transferable: To write the characteristic equation of a new queue, add one operator per independent arrival or service process (argument z for an increase, 1/z for a decrease, the batch generating function for bulk moves) and require the spectrum of the sum to vanish (pp. 12-15).
Extend a stage method beyond rational distributions with elapsed-time supplementary variables and hazard rates (pp. 4-7).

quotes.text: Our results are structural for the case of arbitrary distributions and aim to unify the field, but they can potentially lead to an algorithmic solution for queues with distributions in the class R.
The main difficulty with such an algorithm is not the solution for the roots, but rather that the linear system becomes very large very quickly.
